learn.title: EVs as Grid Helpers
learn.intro: Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology allows electric vehicles to return stored energy to the power grid during peak demand, enhancing grid stability and reducing reliance on fossil fuel plants. This bidirectional energy flow supports renewable integration and creates a decentralized energy network.
learn.c1_text: EVs store renewable energy during off-peak hours and discharge it during peak demand, reducing grid strain. For example, a 60 kWh EV battery can power an average home for 2-3 hours, acting as a mobile power reserve.
learn.c2_text: V2G systems use smart algorithms to schedule charging when electricity is cheap and grid demand is low. This ensures EVs support grid stability without inconveniencing users, balancing supply and demand efficiently.
learn.c3_text: India plans 30% EV penetration by 2030. With 1.5 million EVs projected by 2025, their combined battery capacity could meet 2 GW of peak demand, easing grid stress during summer peaks.
learn.stat1: India’s EV fleet could provide 1.2 GW of aggregated power by 2025 (NITI Aayog)
learn.stat2: Global V2G market to reach $15B by 2028 (McKinsey)
learn.stat3: Tesla’s V2G pilot in California reduced grid peak load by 8% (NREL)
learn.stat4: China’s 1 million EVs could support 5 GW of grid services (IEA)

learn.title: Solar Boom in India
learn.intro: India’s Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme aims to make the country a global solar manufacturing hub by offering financial incentives to domestic manufacturers, reducing import dependence and lowering solar panel costs.
learn.c1_text: The PLI scheme offers up to 40% incentives on module manufacturing and 15% on cell production. This has attracted ₹17,000 crore in investments from companies like Adani and Tata Power.
learn.c2_text: Local manufacturing reduces import costs by 20-30%, making solar panels cheaper. For example, a 5 MW plant built locally could save ₹10-15 crores compared to imported panels.
learn.c3_text: India aims for 500 GW renewable capacity by 2030. The PLI scheme targets 10 GW annual domestic solar cell and module manufacturing by 2025, aligning with national goals.
learn.stat1: India’s solar capacity reached 63 GW by 2024 (MNRE)
learn.stat3: India imported ₹1.2 lakh crore worth of solar panels in 2023 (CEPC)
learn.stat4: Local manufacturing could cut panel costs by 25% by 2025 (Bridgwater)

learn.title: The Duck Curve Problem
learn.intro: Solar energy’s rapid growth creates a ‘duck curve’—a sharp drop in grid demand during midday (when solar is abundant) followed by a steep evening peak, challenging grid operators to balance supply and demand.
learn.c1_text: At noon, solar can meet 80% of demand, but by 7 PM, demand surges 50% as solar fades. This creates a ‘ramp rate’ of 10 GW/hour in California, requiring fast-response power sources.
learn.c2_text: Energy storage can smooth the duck curve by charging during solar surplus and discharging during evening peaks. For example, a 100 MW battery can offset 300 MW of fossil fuel plants during peak hours.
learn.c3_text: India’s solar capacity could cause similar issues. With 63 GW solar by 2024, the evening ramp rate may reach 5 GW/hour by 2030, requiring grid modernization and storage solutions.
learn.stat1: California’s duck curve ramp rate: 10 GW/hour (DOE)
learn.stat2: India’s solar ramp rate projected at 5 GW/hour by 2030 (CEPC)
learn.stat3: Germany’s battery storage to reach 10 GW by 2025 (IEA)
learn.stat4: India’s grid needs ₹2 lakh crore for upgrades by 2030 (MNRE)

learn.title: Wind Turbine Lifespan
learn.intro: Wind turbines last 20-25 years, but blade recycling remains a challenge. Innovations in blade design and recycling processes are critical to ensure sustainable wind energy growth.
learn.c1_text: Modern blades use recyclable materials like thermoplastic resins. For example, Vestas’ recyclable blades can be ground into raw materials for new products, reducing landfill waste.
learn.c2_text: Turbine components are disassembled, and materials like steel (95% recyclable) and copper (90%) are recovered. Blade recycling costs are expected to drop 30% by 2030 with new technologies.
learn.c3_text: India’s 40 GW wind capacity by 2024 will generate 10,000+ tons of blade waste annually. The government’s 2023 policy mandates 70% blade recycling by 2030, supporting circular economy goals.
learn.stat1: Global wind blade waste: 2.3 million tons by 2030 (IRENA)

learn.title: Green Steel Revolution
learn.intro: Green steel production uses hydrogen instead of coal in blast furnaces, cutting CO2 emissions by 90%. This technology is vital for decarbonizing the steel industry, which accounts for 7% of global emissions.
learn.c1_text: Hydrogen replaces coke in reducing iron ore, producing water vapor instead of CO2. A 1000-ton steel plant using green hydrogen can cut 500 tons of CO2 annually, equivalent to 100,000 trees.
learn.c2_text: Hybrid systems combine hydrogen with traditional methods. For example, SSAB’s HYBRIT project in Sweden uses 100% green hydrogen, achieving 90% emission cuts while maintaining production efficiency.
learn.c3_text: India’s steel sector aims for 50% green steel by 2030. The government’s National Hydrogen Mission plans to deploy 5 GW of green hydrogen electrolyzers by 2030, supporting domestic steel decarbonization.

learn.title: Green Bonds for Clean Energy
learn.intro: Green bonds finance renewable energy projects by offering investors returns linked to climate goals. They mobilize capital for solar, wind, and storage, driving global energy transition efforts.
learn.c1_text: Green bonds fund projects like India’s 500 GW renewable target. For example, a $1 billion green bond could finance 10 GW of solar farms, with returns tied to emission reductions.
learn.c2_text: The global green bond market reached $700 billion in 2023. India’s green bond issuance grew 40% in 2023, with ₹10,000 crore raised for solar and wind projects.
learn.c3_text: India’s first green bond in 2015 raised ₹1,000 crore for solar projects. By 2023, the country had issued ₹30,000 crore in green bonds, funding 15 GW of renewable energy capacity.
